newsitem.title: JAPAN: DKB set for more turmoil in Japan payoff scandal.
newsitem.headline: DKB set for more turmoil in Japan payoff scandal.

text.p: Investigations into massive loans by Dai-Ichi Kangyo Bank Ltd (DKB) to a racketeer-linked firm may be leading to a breach of trust charge against one of Japan's top banks, industry sources said on Tuesday.

But unlike Nomura Securities Co Ltd, which is tangled up in the same racketeer payoff scandal, the damage to DKB will be largely limited to its reputation, with little immediate impact on its bottom line, the sources said.

DKB has admitted to extending loans to a company run by the younger brother of "sokaiya" corporate racketeer Ryuichi Koike and to concealing those deals during Ministry of Finance (MOF) inspections in 1990 and 1994.

The loans, which in themselves were not illegal, were provided through DKB's general affairs section. The general affairs sections of Japanese companies are traditionally believed to handle any dealings with racketeers.

The Tokyo Shimbun newspaper reported over the weekend that prosecutors are currently questioning DKB executives on suspicion that the 1994 loans, which were uncollateralised, violated the Commercial Code or involved a breach of trust.
Prosecutors and a DKB spokesman would not comment on the Tokyo Shimbun report.
The two Koike brothers were arrested last month on suspicion of taking about 50 million yen ($431,000) in illegal payments from Nomura Securities.

Sokaiya buy shares in companies to gain access to their shareholder meetings, and then threaten to disrupt the meetings unless they are paid off. Japan's Commercial Code bans Japanese firms from making such payoffs.

A report by MOF last week said some of DKB's loans to a firm owned by the younger Koike, Yoshinori, were used by the elder Koike, the sokaiya, to buy shares in Japan's "Big Four" brokerages, including Nomura.
Yoshinori Koike and his company received a total of 27.5 billion yen ($237 million) in loans from DKB, the report said.
The bank announced the resignations of its president, Katushiko Kondo, and its chairman, Kuniji Miyazaki, on May 23 to take responsibility for the revelations of sokaiya links.

But Ichiro Fujita, the current vice president who is to take the helm from Kondo in June, has said he knew of the existence of the loans in question in late 1995, well before DKB revealed the details last month.
Industry sources said that, depending on the outcome of the prosecutors' investigations into management's involvement, another reshuffle at the bank is likely.

Kondo said during parliamentary questioning last week that the bank will fully investigate the possibility that other improper loans were made, and that it will take strict action in response to any misdeeds by DKB officials, including Fujita.
As the the investigation continues, some public entities such as the Tokyo metropolitan government have shown their displeasure with DKB by withdrawing public funds under its management.
Regional governments, including the prefectures of Yamagata, Tochigi and Oita, have also withdrawn their deposits at DKB, The Nihon Keizai Shimbun newspaper said on Tuesday.
But analysts said these actions will have only a marginal effect on DKB, which has more than two trillion yen ($17.2 billion) in annual revenues.

"The Finance Ministry will impose administrative penalties against DKB and order it to improve its operations, but it is impossible to suspend DKB's banking business," said one banking analyst. ($=116 yen)
